variants.title: Choose the method shape
variants.context: gRPC has four method shapes: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Choose by who sends how many messages and when each side can act.
variants.prompt: A service looks up one account by ID and returns it. Which method shape?
optionFeedback: One bounded request, one response, then final status.
Streaming adds lifecycle for a single bounded result.
Two independent streams are far more than a lookup needs.
variants.hint: How many messages flow in each direction?
variants.explanation: Unary is the default for bounded commands and lookups.

variants.title: Choose the method shape
variants.context: gRPC has four method shapes: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Choose by who sends how many messages and when each side can act.
variants.prompt: A client uploads a large file in chunks and wants one confirmation at the end. Which shape?
options: Unary with the whole file in one message.
optionFeedback: Many client messages, one server response after the client finishes; define partial-upload behavior.
One huge message defeats flow control and buffers everything.
The server is not the one sending many messages.
variants.explanation: Client streaming fits uploads and incremental aggregation.

variants.title: Choose the method shape
variants.context: gRPC has four method shapes: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Choose by who sends how many messages and when each side can act.
variants.prompt: One query yields an ordered sequence of events too large to buffer in one response. Which shape?
options: Server streaming; the client must consume or cancel.
Unary with pagination inside the response.
optionFeedback: One request, many ordered responses over time.
Pagination hides the stream and still buffers each page.
The client sends one request here.
variants.explanation: Within one RPC, messages preserve order per direction. Across RPCs, do not infer global order.

variants.title: Evolve the message
variants.context: Field numbers identify fields on the wire and are part of the compatibility contract. Add with new numbers, deploy tolerant readers, migrate behavior, then reserve removed numbers and names; never reuse them.
variants.prompt: A message needs a new field. Put the compatible-growth steps in order.

items.text: Add the field with a new number and define behavior when it is absent.
Deploy readers that understand both shapes before writers depend on it.
Migrate callers gradually and watch defaults, unknown enums, and JSON boundaries.
When a field is retired, reserve its number and old name forever.

variants.explanation: Add → tolerant readers → migrate → reserve. Reusing a number makes old bytes ambiguous.

variants.title: Evolve the message
variants.context: Field numbers identify fields on the wire and are part of the compatibility contract. Add with new numbers, deploy tolerant readers, migrate behavior, then reserve removed numbers and names; never reuse them.
variants.prompt: A field is being removed. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Add any replacement field with a fresh number.
Roll out code that tolerates the field’s absence.
Move callers off the old field and observe.
Reserve the retired number and name; never recycle them.

variants.hint: Removal ends with a reservation, not a deletion.
variants.explanation: Deleted field numbers and names should be reserved so no future field can reinterpret old data.

variants.title: Evolve the message
variants.context: Field numbers identify fields on the wire and are part of the compatibility contract. Add with new numbers, deploy tolerant readers, migrate behavior, then reserve removed numbers and names; never reuse them.
variants.prompt: An enum gains new values. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Add the values; keep the zero value in place.
Deploy clients that tolerate values from newer writers.
Move writers to emit the new values and observe unknown-value handling.

variants.hint: Clients must tolerate unknown values before writers send them.
variants.explanation: An enum needs a zero value, and old clients must survive new values introduced by newer writers.

variants.title: Budget the call
variants.context: gRPC sets no deadline by default. A retry is a new attempt inside the same overall deadline; remaining deadline is the original minus completed attempts and backoff. Maximum attempts includes the original attempt.
variants.prompt: The call deadline is 2,000 ms. Attempt one used 600 ms and failed with UNAVAILABLE. Backoff before the retry is 200 ms. How much deadline remains for attempt two?
variants.hint: Subtract the attempt and the backoff from the original deadline.
variants.explanation: 2,000 − 600 − 200 = 1,200 ms. A retry is not a fresh budget.

mistakes.feedback: A retry runs inside the same overall deadline.

variants.title: Budget the call
variants.context: gRPC sets no deadline by default. A retry is a new attempt inside the same overall deadline; remaining deadline is the original minus completed attempts and backoff. Maximum attempts includes the original attempt.
variants.prompt: The deadline is 1,500 ms. Two attempts of 500 ms each failed, with backoffs of 100 ms and then 200 ms. How much remains for the third attempt?
variants.hint: Subtract every attempt and every backoff.
variants.explanation: 1,500 − 500 − 100 − 500 − 200 = 200 ms. A downstream call receives only what remains.

variants.title: Budget the call
variants.context: gRPC sets no deadline by default. A retry is a new attempt inside the same overall deadline; remaining deadline is the original minus completed attempts and backoff. Maximum attempts includes the original attempt.
variants.prompt: A retry policy allows a maximum of 3 attempts. How many retries can follow the original attempt?
variants.explanation: 3 attempts = 1 original + 2 retries. More attempts can amplify an outage.

mistakes.feedback: The original attempt is one of the three.
Two retries fit inside three attempts.

variants.title: Read the status
variants.context: Status codes are a stable vocabulary for how one RPC ended: INVALID_ARGUMENT (request invalid regardless of state), FAILED_PRECONDITION (wait for a state fix), ABORTED (restart the sequence), UNAVAILABLE (transient), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (budget expired; effects may have happened), CANCELLED.
variants.prompt: A request has a negative quantity. Which status?
optionFeedback: The request is invalid regardless of system state.
FAILED_PRECONDITION is for state the caller must wait to fix.
Nothing transient happened.
variants.hint: Would the request be valid if the system’s state were different?
variants.explanation: INVALID_ARGUMENT never depends on current state; retrying it is pointless.

variants.title: Read the status
variants.context: Status codes are a stable vocabulary for how one RPC ended: INVALID_ARGUMENT (request invalid regardless of state), FAILED_PRECONDITION (wait for a state fix), ABORTED (restart the sequence), UNAVAILABLE (transient), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (budget expired; effects may have happened), CANCELLED.
variants.prompt: A call fails because the account is still being provisioned. Which status tells the caller to wait rather than retry immediately?
optionFeedback: The caller should wait until an explicit state condition is fixed.
The request itself is fine.
ABORTED means restart a read-modify-write sequence.
variants.hint: Is the request wrong, or is the world not ready?

variants.title: Read the status
variants.context: Status codes are a stable vocabulary for how one RPC ended: INVALID_ARGUMENT (request invalid regardless of state), FAILED_PRECONDITION (wait for a state fix), ABORTED (restart the sequence), UNAVAILABLE (transient), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (budget expired; effects may have happened), CANCELLED.
variants.prompt: A client receives DEADLINE_EXCEEDED on a payment RPC. What can it conclude?
options: Its time budget expired; the server may still have committed the payment.
optionFeedback: A status describes how the RPC ended from one side; server effects may have happened.
A deadline says nothing about the server’s progress.
Assuming failure risks a duplicate on retry.
variants.hint: What does a deadline tell you about the server?
variants.explanation: Query operation state or reconcile instead of guessing that a timeout means no change.

variants.title: Decide the retry
variants.context: Classify effects before enabling retries: read-only lookups are usually retryable within bounds; idempotent mutations need a client-generated operation key; unkeyed mutations must not be retried automatically. Keep retries centralized.
variants.prompt: An unkeyed CreateInvoice RPC returns UNAVAILABLE. Should the client library retry automatically?
options: No. The mutation may already have committed; reconcile or query state instead.
optionFeedback: Without a stable operation key, a retry can duplicate the invoice.
Retryable status does not make the effect safe.
Attempt count does not fix duplication.
variants.hint: What identifies this invoice across attempts?
variants.explanation: Retry safety belongs to the application effect, not the status code.

variants.title: Decide the retry
variants.context: Classify effects before enabling retries: read-only lookups are usually retryable within bounds; idempotent mutations need a client-generated operation key; unkeyed mutations must not be retried automatically. Keep retries centralized.
variants.prompt: A read-only GetPrice RPC fails transiently. Retry?
options: Yes, with bounded attempts, backoff, and the remaining deadline.
optionFeedback: Reads create no second effect, but attempts must still be bounded.
Reads are the safe case for retries.
Unbounded retries amplify outages.
variants.hint: Does a repeated read create a new effect?
variants.explanation: Read-only lookups are usually retryable; bound attempts, backoff, deadline, and amplification.

variants.title: Decide the retry
variants.context: Classify effects before enabling retries: read-only lookups are usually retryable within bounds; idempotent mutations need a client-generated operation key; unkeyed mutations must not be retried automatically. Keep retries centralized.
variants.prompt: SDK, sidecar, proxy, and workflow layers each retry three times. What happens under an outage?
options: Attempts multiply across layers and amplify the outage; centralize retries.
optionFeedback: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 attempts per call is a self-inflicted storm.
Layered retries compound.
Layers do not coordinate.
variants.hint: How many total attempts can one call generate?
variants.explanation: Keep retries centralized and observe call count and attempt count separately.
